subject: art-design
title: Daguerreotype and Early Photography
welcome_lead: 1839: Daguerre announces a process that captures light on silvered copper.
meta_desc: A-Level Art & Design: Daguerreotype, calotype, and the birth of photography.

concepts.def: Daguerre's 1839 silver-iodide photographic process on copper.

walkthroughs.body_html: On 19 August 1839, the French government announced the Daguerreotype process, freely offered to the world (Britain excepted by patent). Photography became public.
In 1841, Henry Fox Talbot patented the calotype — a paper negative permitting multiple positive prints. The negative-positive system, not Daguerre's silver plate, became photography's future.
In 1878, Eadweard Muybridge photographed Leland Stanford's galloping horse with twelve cameras at Palo Alto — proving all four hooves leave the ground simultaneously and anticipating cinema.
